newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Europe to lag U.S. longer term.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Europe to lag U.S. longer term.

text.p: European bond markets may outperform Treasuries in the medium term as prices play catch-up to the recent U.S. rally, partly inspired by Fed Chairman Greenspan's upbeat assessment of the economy, analysts said on Wednesday.
But over the next year or so, they will likely underperform as the economic cycle in Germany and France changes direction and growth and interest rates start heading up, they added.
"In Europe, there's still some catching up to be done with the upswing seen in Treasury prices," said Stephen Lewis, chief economist of London Bond Broking.
"In the medium term -- one to three months -- we will see a widening of the spread between the U.S. and Germany which implies the U.S. will do less well in capital terms."
But Lewis added that on a 12 month view, investors had to consider the state of the economic cycle on both sides of the Atlantic.
"The U.S. economy has every chance of continuing to expand, but we may also see some pick-up in the German economy, which will then lead to a narrowing of the yield spread with Germany," he said.

By 0725 GMT, the 10-year T-note/Bund spread was at 74 basis points, down five basis points from Tuesday's close. The spread has snapped in around 30 basis points in the last two months as the chances of a U.S. interest rate rise have receded.
Treasuries leapt overnight after Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan said the U.S. central bank would raise interest rates if needed to head off inflation, but suggested that might not happen anytime soon.

In his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, Greenspan told Congress the U.S. economy may be undergoing some "basic improvements" thanks to technological advances that were boosting worker producitvity and corporate profits.
U.S. Treasuries lapped up Greenspan's comments, with the 30-year long bond shooting up over a point and a half and the yield dipping to 6.41 percent, its lowest level for more than seven months.
European bond markets obediently followed suit, with German, British, French and Italian markets crashing through highs in early trade.
"The Treasury/Bund spread has come in a long way and that should provide decent support for Bunds," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London.
He said the period of chronic underperformance by Europe had probably come to an end for the time being since the growth picture in Europe was still not particularly strong.

"That spread won't do an awful lot -- but if anything, Treasuries are still slightly better value than Bunds given U.S. inflation will probably trend down and German inflation will stay the same," he said.
Analysts said the degree of underperformance by European bond markets longer term depended on the relative growth profiles in the U.S. and Europe.
"It will depend very much on how strong the upturn in Europe is and precisely what happens in the U.S. economy," said Lewis.

Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International Europe, agreed that on a 12 month view, European bond markets would enjoy a firmer tone but would underperform the U.S. as the Fed takes its foot off the monetary brake and people start talking of a U.S. rate cut.
"I'm looking for long-term gains in all European markets in the context of underperformance," he said.
Richardson expected the 10-year T-note/Bund spread to be virtually flat on a 12 month view.
"If we're right and are back to 1960s (inflation levels) then yields can go back to those levels too," said Richardson, noting the 30-year yield fell to below five percent.
"I'm not saying we'll get down to four percent, but certainly something below six percent is quite credible."
